title: Tunnel of Hope: The Line Beneath the Runway
listening_note: A 12-minute guide to Sarajevo's Tunnel D-B, where a narrow passage became a crucial line of survival during the siege.
story_html:
Begin at the entrance, not with the legend

Before you enter, pause at the Butmir-side entrance. The official name of this place is Tunnel D-B. In public memory it is more often called the Tunnel of Hope. Both names matter. One sounds like a piece of wartime engineering, a code on a plan. The other carries the meaning people have given it since: connection, endurance, a line that made life in a besieged city less impossible.

The first thing to keep in mind is that you are not about to walk the entire wartime tunnel. The Memorial Center preserves the original entrance on this side and an authentic twenty-five-metre section, followed by a revitalised hundred metres of the original tunnel tube. That is enough to change your sense of scale. But it is not the whole eight-hundred-metre passage that ran beneath Sarajevo Airport's runway in 1993.

So let the central question for this visit be a practical one: what does a city do when a runway has become a barrier, and a route underneath it becomes necessary for survival? The answer is not a simple story of escape. It is a story about labour, logistics, danger, civilian life, military necessity, and the way a place later learns to remember all of that.

A runway that divided a city

In the early 1990s, Sarajevo was under siege. The airport runway lay between areas held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Dobrinja on one side and Butmir on the other. It was not an ordinary transit zone. Crossing the exposed airport area could be fatal. The city needed a route that could move beneath that line instead of across it.

By July 1993, Tunnel D-B was operating under the runway. It linked the besieged city to territory outside the encirclement. The space was roughly one metre wide and about one and a half metres high. Its low dimensions are not a dramatic detail added after the fact. They tell you what kind of infrastructure this was. It was not made for comfort, ceremony, or a swift exit. It was a constrained corridor, dug to do a job that no normal road could do.

Try not to picture it as a secret shortcut in a thriller. The evidence points to something more demanding. The tunnel became a route for civilians, soldiers, humanitarian aid, and supplies. It was one of the systems that allowed a city to keep functioning when ordinary systems had been cut apart. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia records both civilian and military use. That distinction is important. Calling it only a civilian escape route makes the history easier to tell, but less true.

Even the name Tunnel of Hope needs a little care. It is a powerful local memorial name, and it deserves to be heard as such. But hope here did not mean safety. It meant the possibility of connection under conditions in which every connection carried risk.

Building a route for the things a city needs

Now imagine the original tunnel not as a single dramatic line on a map but as a working system. It needed people to dig, shore up, carry, organise, and move. The Memorial Center's exhibition includes plans, orders, rare footage, photographs of people involved in construction, and tools used during the building work. The point is not to turn the builders into anonymous heroes. It is to notice that survival depended on skilled, repetitive work done under pressure.

Once the passage was functioning, it carried more than people. Official Sarajevo material describes rails and cargo carts, along with a telephone cable, a high-voltage cable, and a fuel pipeline. These details give the tunnel its real meaning. A city under siege does not survive on symbolism. It needs communication, electricity, fuel, medicine, food, movement, and ways to keep institutions and households connected to one another.

There is a temptation, when visiting a narrow historical space, to make claustrophobia the whole story. The passage is indeed narrow. But the stronger image is coordination. Somebody had to decide what went through first. Somebody had to carry a load or wait in line. Somebody had to maintain the route. The tunnel's importance came from this accumulation of practical decisions, repeated day after day.

That is also why its story cannot be separated from the siege outside. The Tribunal's record notes that the tunnel entrances and exits were frequently shelled by Bosnian Serb forces. The dangerous part was not confined to the underground section. Reaching it, leaving it, and moving anything through it were all part of the risk. The tunnel reduced one kind of exposure. It did not end the conditions that made it necessary.

In the Memorial Center, look for the objects that seem least grand: improvised household items, food from humanitarian assistance, photographs of daily life. They keep the tunnel from becoming only an engineering achievement. A connection under the runway mattered because people above ground still had to make meals, obtain supplies, care for family, communicate, and improvise a life. Infrastructure and ordinary life were inseparable.

Hope, but not a fairy tale

The word hope can sound uncomplicated from a distance. At this site, it should not. The tunnel connected people to supplies and to one another, and its existence became a powerful symbol of Sarajevo's resistance and endurance. But it was also part of a war. It served the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as civilians and humanitarian movement. It did not undo hunger, bereavement, displacement, or the violence of the siege.

This is why it is worth holding two thoughts at once. First, the tunnel was a crucial route of survival. Second, a memorial name can never carry every part of a historical reality. A scholarly study of the site describes Tunnel D-B as difficult heritage: a place where resilience and a traumatic past have to share the same physical space. Another study of Sarajevo's museums notes that exhibitions about the siege often foreground civilian everyday life rather than the wider military and political context. That is not a reason to distrust the museum. It is a reason to read its choices carefully.

As you move through the displays, ask: what is this object helping me see, and what does it leave outside the frame? A map of the siege explains why a route beneath the runway was needed. A can of humanitarian food makes scarcity concrete. A tool or a construction order makes the tunnel's creation less abstract. None of these objects is the whole war. Together, they show how a city had to think in material terms just to remain connected.

That kind of attention respects the people whose lives are being remembered. It avoids converting suffering into scenery, and it avoids the opposite mistake of treating the tunnel as a clean, uplifting metaphor. The history is more difficult and more human than either version.

What remains, and what has been rebuilt

There is another distinction to notice: original and restored. The current visitor route includes an authentic twenty-five metres of tunnel and a revitalised hundred metres whose structural elements were replaced so that it evokes the interior as it functioned between 1993 and 1995. That does not make the experience false. It tells you plainly that memorial sites have to preserve, stabilise, and interpret fragile places if people are going to encounter them at all.

The difference is useful. An untouched ruin can seem to promise direct access to the past. A restored passage makes its mediation visible. You are not travelling back to 1993. You are standing in a place where traces of 1993 have been protected and arranged so that their meaning can be carried forward. The Memorial Center has managed the complex since 2012, and its interpretation connects the tunnel to the wider siege of Sarajevo.

If you have time, look closely at the siege map in the exhibition. The Memorial Center overlays the siege on a map of Olympic Sarajevo from 1984. The contrast makes a useful point without needing sentiment. A city recently presented to the world through sport had, within a decade, been turned into a place where a route beneath an airport was necessary. The map does not explain every political cause or every person's experience. It does help you see why logistics became part of daily life and why a tunnel could become a public symbol.

That is why the site works best when you give it two kinds of attention. One is physical: notice the height of the ceiling, the width of the passage, the distance your body can cover in a few steps. The other is ethical: notice the care with which a local institution asks visitors to connect that small physical space to a much larger story without pretending that a visit can contain it.

Memory is never neutral, especially after a war. But neither is forgetting. The Tunnel of Hope survives because people decided that this piece of wartime infrastructure should be held in public view, not allowed to disappear into a private plot by the airport or into an anecdote repeated without evidence.

Return to the surface with a different scale

Before you leave, return your attention to the entrance. Think of the original length beneath the runway, then of the short section you have walked. The gap between them is not a failure of the museum. It is the point. No preserved fragment can reproduce the full exhaustion, fear, organisation, and improvisation of a city under siege. What it can do is make those things harder to reduce to a headline.

Carry one question back into Sarajevo: what kinds of work allow ordinary life to continue when ordinary routes disappear? You may notice the city differently after this. Not because the tunnel gives you a single lesson, but because it turns connection itself into something visible: power lines, food deliveries, phone calls, roads, a friend making it home. In 1993, under this runway, connection had to be dug by hand and sustained at risk. That is what the name hope is asking you to remember.
